summary: On a mission to the Moon or Mars, a doctor on Earth is minutes away by radio, so astronauts must notice and act on health problems themselves. For the challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions", we built MEGA Health, an interactive health bridge for each crew member. The astronaut clicks a 3D body: every body zone is coloured green (normal), yellow (moderate) or red (critical) from its readings, and the head, heart, lungs, arms and legs open a 3D view of the organ or muscles inside. Each zone explains, in plain language, which measurements can be taken in space, why they matter, how NASA's spaceflight hazards affect them, who should act (the astronaut, the crew, or the flight surgeon on Earth) and what to do now. A hazard simulator shows how a solar flare, a spacewalk or skipped exercise would hit the body; daily countermeasure quests raise a mission-readiness score; and Ask MEGA, a voice assistant running on a local AI with no link to Earth, answers health questions from the astronaut's own record. This matters because on long missions the crew is the first line of medical care: MEGA Health turns many numbers into one glance, one tap and one clear next step.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

MEGA Health is a web application ("the bridge") that lets each astronaut assess their own health and decide what to do. Main use: an astronaut opens their profile, sees at a glance which body zones are yellow or red, taps one to understand the problem and follows the recommended countermeasure — or escalates to the flight surgeon when the reading is red.

WORKING FEATURES (all in the live project)

- 3D astronaut with 12 clickable body zones (head, eyes, heart, lungs, abdomen, back & spine, upper arms, forearms, hands, thighs, calves, feet), each coloured green / yellow / red from its readings.

- Inside view: clicking the head, heart, lungs, an arm or a leg flies the camera into the body; the skin fades and the brain, heart, lungs or the limb's muscles appear in place.

- Zone panel: every reading with its value, normal range and status; a trend chart over mission days; "Why this exam matters"; "How to measure" with the onboard device; the zone's hazards; countermeasures; and an "Earth medical spinoff" note.

- Triage that says who acts: green = self-care, yellow = crew countermeasure, red = ground flight-surgeon consult. Red zones can queue a telemetry packet to the flight surgeon, showing the 4 min 44 s one-way radio delay (simulated).

- Mission readiness score (0–100) from the database formula, raised by starting countermeasures and completing daily quests, lowered by hazards.

- Space hazard simulator: solar particle event, 6-hour spacewalk, 60 days without exercise — shows which zones degrade and the real change in readiness.

- Daily countermeasure quests with streaks and XP (gamification).

- Crew overview: 5 astronauts, sleep chart, vital-sign trends (heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, blood sugar, mood), cabin environment (pressure, O2, CO2, temperature, noise), space weather and the CSA CANS neutron-dose reading.

- Ask MEGA voice assistant (local only): speak a question, hear the answer. It runs on Bionic, a local AI app, with the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 4B model, and is briefed with the astronaut's readings, normal ranges and statuses so its answers come from the record.

HOW IT WORKS AND HOW THE DATA SUPPORTS IT

The team built a SQLite astronaut health database (11 tables) with 5 crew profiles, 12 body zones and 53 health metrics. Each metric has units, green/amber thresholds, trend history, "why it matters" and "how to measure" text, written from the NASA Human Research Program and Canadian Space Agency resources. A Python script exports it to JSON for the website. Zone colours come from the thresholds; readiness follows the database formula (100 − 5 per amber metric − 20 per red metric, kept between 0 and 100), and the live readiness logic is checked by an automated test of every astronaut × hazard × quest combination (about 40,000 checks). The 3D body was split into the 12 zones in Blender.

BENEFITS

Fast self-assessment (colour → tap → action), clear escalation rules that save scarce radio time, plain-language education so astronauts don't need to be doctors, and an assistant that works with no Earth link. The same approach fits remote clinics, polar stations and ships on Earth.

LIMITATIONS

- All readings are simulated mission data; no live sensors are connected and there is no manual data-entry screen yet.

- It is decision support, not a medical device; red results always point to the flight surgeon.

- Ask MEGA needs the Bionic local AI on the same computer and Chrome or Edge for voice, so it is not available in the online version; answers take about 8–20 seconds.

- The telemetry packet to the flight surgeon is simulated.

- Designed for desktop/laptop screens.

FUTURE PLANS

Connect wearables and onboard devices and add manual entry with measurement reminders; a flight-surgeon dashboard that syncs over the delayed link; personal baselines and early-warning trend detection; an offline installable version for ship hardware with a smaller, faster on-board model; clinical validation and more languages.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

JavaScript (React 19, Vite), CSS, three.js with React Three Fiber, drei and three-mesh-bvh, Draco 3D compression, Python and SQLite (database), Blender 5.2 (3D processing), FFmpeg (video), Bionic local AI app with NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 4B, Web Speech API, Git and GitHub (code), Cloudflare Pages (hosting).
